title: Git Branching Without Fear
author: Kabir Nair
excerpt: A mental model for branches, merges, and rebases that finally made it click for our workshop attendees.
content:
Most people are scared of git because they think of it as a stack of magic commands instead of a graph of snapshots. Once you draw the graph on paper, branching stops being scary.

Start every new feature with a branch named after the change, not the ticket number. Commit small, commit often, and write commit messages as if you're explaining the change to a teammate who wasn't in the room.

When you're ready to merge, prefer rebasing your feature branch onto the latest main before opening a pull request. It keeps history linear and makes code review far easier to follow.

title: What We Learned Running a 150-Person Hackathon
author: Sana Iyer
excerpt: Logistics notes from Orbit 2026, for anyone planning their own campus hackathon.
content:
Food ran out at hour 14 last year, so this year we over-ordered by 20% and it was almost exactly right. Lesson one: always over-order.

We also split judging into two rounds, a quick pitch round for all teams and a longer round for the top 15. It cut total judging time in half without losing quality of feedback.

The biggest win was assigning a mentor to every 5 teams instead of leaving mentors to roam. Teams used mentor time far more once it felt like it was theirs.

title: How to Pick Your First Side Project
author: Diya Mehta
excerpt: The three questions we ask every new member before they open a code editor.
content:
Before you write a line of code, answer three questions: who is this for, what do they do today without it, and why would they switch.

A project that solves a real problem for five people you know will teach you more than a clone of an app used by millions. It also gives you something honest to talk about in an interview.

Start small enough to finish in two weeks. Momentum matters more than scope in the first project.
